s: A scrum team's daily stand-up has turned into a status report to the project manager. What should the PM do?
o: Keep attending to gather status for your own reports
Step back and coach the team to own the stand-up
Swap it for a written status report sent each morning
Move the stand-up to weekly so it takes less time
e: The daily stand-up belongs to the team. A servant leader coaches the team to own it rather than using it for management reporting.

s: Two stakeholders give you contradictory requirements for the same feature. Both are senior. What is the BEST action?
o: Wait for one of the two stakeholders to back down before you decide
Build what the more senior stakeholder asked for to avoid friction
Facilitate a needs-based discussion, with the sponsor as tiebreaker
Build both versions and let users choose after the first release
e: Resolve conflicting requirements through facilitation focused on needs and business value. Escalate to the sponsor only if they cannot agree.

s: A new team member is productive but does not take part in team discussions. What is the BEST first step?
o: Ask them to speak up during the next team discussion
Note the lack of participation in their performance review
Leave it alone while their individual output stays strong
Talk privately to learn what would help them contribute
e: Understand the reason privately first. Contributions can be limited by culture, confidence or team norms.

s: A key user keeps saying the delivered increments do not match what they meant, though they approved the stories. What addresses the root cause BEST?
o: Agree acceptance criteria early and demo working examples
Add a formal sign-off form that the user completes for every story
Ask the user to read each story more carefully before approving it
Hold increments back and demo everything only near the very end
e: Shared understanding comes from collaboration and clear acceptance criteria, not bureaucracy.

s: A team lacks confidence after a failed release. Which action is MOST appropriate for the project leader?
o: Cut the next release's scope without discussing it with the team
Run a blameless review, recognise wins and agree improvements
Replace the team lead who owned the failed release
Identify who caused the failure, document it and move on
e: A blameless retrospective rebuilds trust and turns failure into learning.

s: Your team is overloaded and you have been asked to add a feature. Team members say they cannot take on more. What do you do?
o: Ask the team to work overtime to fit the new feature in
Add the feature and let the delivery date slip without comment
Show capacity data and trade-offs to the decision maker
Trim testing effort so the feature fits in the iteration
e: Make trade-offs visible and let the decision maker choose. Do not hide impact or cut quality silently.

s: A team member complains that a colleague takes credit for shared work. What is the BEST response?
o: Tell the two colleagues to sort it out between themselves
Restructure the team so their work no longer overlaps
Formally reprimand the colleague who is said to take credit
Hear both sides, then facilitate a talk about contribution
e: Hear both sides before acting, then facilitate. Immediate discipline without facts is unfair.

s: Which is a characteristic of a high-performing team?
o: Strong reliance on the PM's decisions
High trust and open communication
Avoidance of open disagreement
Strict separation of individual tasks
e: High-performing teams are interdependent, trust each other and communicate openly, including productive disagreement.

s: You discover that a vendor's gift to a team member could look like an attempt to influence a procurement decision. What do you do?
o: Treat it as harmless because it was a small personal gift
Cancel the vendor's contract at once as a precaution
Share the gift out among the whole team to keep it fair
Follow the conflict policy, report the gift and disclose it
e: PMI's code requires avoiding and disclosing conflicts of interest. Follow the organisation's policy and be transparent.

s: The sponsor has stopped attending steering meetings and decisions are stalling. What do you do FIRST?
o: Escalate the absence to the CEO to restore sponsor attention
Meet the sponsor to learn why and agree how they stay involved
Take the stalled decisions yourself to keep the work moving
Cancel the steering meetings and report by email instead
e: Talk to the sponsor first to find out why and agree an engagement approach.

s: A hybrid project has a predictive hardware phase and an agile software team. The two groups use different reporting. What do you do?
o: Tailor a shared cadence and integration points with joint measures
Make the agile team follow the predictive plan and reporting
Report each group separately and let the sponsor reconcile them
Move the whole project to agile delivery for consistency
e: Hybrid delivery calls for tailoring: shared milestones and integration points with metrics each side can feed.

s: A virtual team member's camera is always off and they rarely respond. What should you do?
o: Refer them to HR for failing to engage with the team
Give them less work until they become more responsive
Check in one-to-one and agree communication expectations
Require everyone to keep their camera on during meetings
e: Find the cause. Agreements, not mandates, are the first step.

s: BAC is $800,000. At the status date PV is $400,000, EV is $360,000 and AC is $400,000. What is the TCPI to meet BAC?
EV is $90,000 and PV is $100,000. What is the schedule variance?
e: SV = EV − PV = −$10,000. SPI is the ratio 0.90.

s: A threat is accepted passively. Where should it appear?
o: Only in the lessons learned log for use on future projects
Nowhere, because passive acceptance involves no action
In the risk register, marked as accepted, with a reserve note
Only in the issue log until the risk actually occurs
e: Accepted risks stay in the register, and active acceptance may establish a contingency reserve.

s: The project team decides to buy insurance against a facility failure. Which response strategy is this?
o: Mitigate
Escalate
Accept
Transfer
e: Insurance transfers the financial impact to a third party.

s: The customer asks for an extra report that was not in the requirements. It is small and the team could do it in a day. What do you do?
o: Decline it because it was never part of the requirements
Add it as a goodwill gesture since it only takes a day
Have the team build it in their own time without logging it
Raise it through change control despite its small size
e: Even small additions are changes. Gold plating and unmanaged scope creep damage trust and the baseline.

s: Which technique shortens the schedule by doing sequential activities in parallel, increasing risk?
o: Fast tracking the activities
Crashing the critical activities
Levelling resources across tasks
Trimming critical path scope
e: Fast tracking overlaps activities and raises rework risk. Crashing adds resources and cost.

s: Resource levelling extends the project end date. What is the effect on the critical path?
o: No effect, since levelling only moves resource assignments
It can create a new resource-constrained critical path
It shortens the critical path by smoothing resource peaks
It removes all float from the non-critical activities
e: Levelling can lengthen the schedule and alter the critical path to a resource critical path.

s: A control chart shows seven consecutive points on one side of the mean, all within control limits. What does this suggest?
o: A non-random pattern: look for an assignable cause
Nothing, since every point is inside the limits
The control limits are set too wide for this process
The process is stable and in statistical control
e: The rule of seven indicates a non-random trend even when points are within limits.

s: A seller disputes a charge and the parties cannot agree. What is the PREFERRED order of resolution?
o: Arbitration, then negotiation, then litigation
Litigation, then mediation, then negotiation
Negotiation, mediation, arbitration, litigation
Escalate to sponsor, then go to litigation
e: Negotiate first, then mediation, then arbitration, with litigation as a last resort.

s: A team's velocity averages 24 points. The backlog has 144 points. About how many iterations are needed?
o: 4 iterations
6 iterations
8 iterations
12 iterations
e: 144 / 24 = 6 iterations, assuming stable velocity.

s: A product owner changes the order of backlog items every other day. The team complains about churn. What should the PM encourage?
o: Hand backlog ordering to the team instead of the product owner
Freeze the backlog order for the entire life of the project
Ask the sponsor to replace the product owner with someone steadier
Agree priorities change between iterations, not during them
e: Protecting the iteration commitment gives stability while keeping flexibility between iterations.

s: A change was approved by the change control board. What is the next step?
o: Update baselines and plans, implement it and tell stakeholders
Record it in lessons learned and move on to the next request
Mark the request closed in the log once the board has signed it
Hold off implementing until the customer asks for the change
e: Approved changes require updates to the affected baselines and communication.

s: You realise a team member already implemented a change that was never approved. What do you do?
o: Refer the team member to HR right away for bypassing control
Approve it retroactively so the records match the work done
Assess its impact and run it through change control
Reverse the change and leave the matter out of the reports
e: Treat it transparently: assess impact, run change control, and fix the process gap.

s: Which document identifies stakeholders and records their requirements, expectations and classification?
o: Project charter
Stakeholder register
Communication log
Lessons register
e: The stakeholder register holds identification, assessment and classification.

s: At project close the customer refuses to formally accept a deliverable that meets the acceptance criteria, saying they want a new feature. What do you do?
o: Show the criteria are met and treat the new ask as a change
Take the dispute to legal straight away to force acceptance
Add the new feature so that the customer will finally accept
Close the project without formal acceptance of the deliverable
e: Hold to the agreed criteria. New wishes are changes, not a reason to withhold acceptance.

s: The project is on time and budget, but the market has shifted and the benefits no longer justify it. What should the PM do?
o: Stop the project immediately because the benefits have gone
Carry on, since the project is on time and on budget
Trim scope quietly to bring the cost down to the new value
Tell the sponsor and governance so they can decide the path
e: Business value drives continuation. Raise it with the sponsor and the steering committee.

s: Your project must meet a security standard not in the original scope. The audit is in six weeks. What do you do?
o: Ask the auditor to waive the standard for this project
Assess impact, raise a change request and plan with security
Defer the work and deal with the findings after the audit
Drop the feature that triggers the standard from the scope
e: Compliance is a constraint. Assess, raise it through change control, and plan.

s: Which is the BEST measure of project success after closure?
o: Whether intended benefits and value are realised
The count of change requests raised during the project
How satisfied the team was with the project experience
That the project was finished on or before the date
e: Delivering business value is the ultimate measure. Time and cost are constraints.
